2.2.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define depolarization and repolarization in cardiac electrophysiology.

●       Understand the relationship between electrical activity and myocardial contraction/relaxation.

●       Correlate depolarization and repolarization with ECG waveforms.

●       Relate these concepts to pacemaker sensing, pacing capture, and arrhythmia recognition.

2.2.1.H2 Explanation

2.2.1.C2 The heart’s ability to beat and pump blood depends entirely on electrical activity occurring at the cellular level. Every heartbeat begins when cardiac cells undergo changes in electrical charge across their membranes. These changes allow electrical impulses to form and spread throughout the myocardium, causing coordinated contraction and relaxation of the heart muscle.

Two of the most fundamental electrical processes in the heart are:

1.    Depolarization

2.    Repolarization

These processes occur continuously with every heartbeat and form the basis of all electrical rhythm generation, ECG interpretation, pacing, and arrhythmia management.

To understand depolarization and repolarization, learners must first understand that every cardiac cell has an electrical charge difference across its membrane, called the membrane potential.

Subtopic 1: Resting Membrane Potential- Polarization

At rest, myocardial cells maintain a negative electrical charge inside the cell compared with outside compared to the outside, the cell is said to be in a polarized state.

This polarized resting state prepares the cell for the next electrical impulse.

Subtopic 2: What Is Depolarization?

Depolarization is the process by which the inside of the cardiac cell becomes less negative and more positive, initiating electrical activation. It is the event that initiates contraction of cardiac muscle.

Subtopic 3: Mechanism of Depolarization

The steps of depolarization are:

Step 1: Threshold Reached A stimulus raises membrane potential to threshold.

Step 2: Sodium Channels Open Rapid influx of sodium ions occurs.

Step 3: Positive Charge Increases Cell interior becomes positive.

Step 4: Action Potential Generated Electrical impulse spreads across myocardium.

This electrical activation then triggers: Muscle contraction

Subtopic 4: Clinical Meaning of Depolarization

Depolarization directly causes:

Electrical Activation

Myocardium becomes electrically stimulated.

Mechanical Contraction

Cardiac muscle contracts after depolarization.

Without depolarization:

●       No contraction occurs

●       No heartbeat occurs

This is why pacemakers function by artificially causing depolarization.

Subtopic 5: What Is Repolarization?

Repolarization is the process by which the cardiac cell returns to its resting negative electrical state after depolarization. it restores the cell’s readiness for the next heartbeat.

Subtopic 6: Mechanism of Repolarization

Steps include:

Step 1: Sodium Channels Close No further sodium entry.

Step 2: Potassium Channels Open Potassium leaves the cell.

Step 3: Cell Interior Becomes Negative Again Returns toward resting potential.

Step 4: Cell Ready for Next Beat Membrane restored to polarized state.

 

Subtopic 7: Relationship to Contraction and Relaxation

Electrical and mechanical activity are linked:

Depolarization → Contraction

Electrical stimulation triggers contraction.

Repolarization → Relaxation

Electrical reset allows relaxation.

This relationship is known as:

Electromechanical Coupling

Subtopic 8: ECG Correlation

Depolarization and repolarization create ECG waveforms.

P Wave

Represents:  Atrial depolarization

QRS Complex

Represents: Ventricular depolarization

T Wave

Represents: Ventricular repolarization

 

Atrial repolarization is usually hidden within the QRS complex.

Subtopic 9: Why Repolarization Is Important

Without repolarization:

●       Cells cannot depolarize again

●       Rhythm would stop

Proper repolarization ensures:

●       Rhythm regularity

●       Prevention of arrhythmias

●       Cellular recovery

Abnormal repolarization may cause:

●       QT prolongation

●       Ventricular arrhythmias

●       Sudden cardiac death

Subtopic 10: Refractory Period

After depolarization:
Cells temporarily cannot depolarize again.

This period is called: Refractory Period

Purpose:

●       Prevents premature reactivation

●       Prevents tetanic contraction

●       Maintains rhythm regularity

 

Subtopic 11: Relevance in Pacemaker Therapy

Pacemakers rely on depolarization and repolarization principles:

Pacing Pulse

Artificially causes depolarization.

Sensing: Detects natural depolarization.

Capture: Occurs when pacing causes depolarization.

Refractory Programming: Prevents oversensing inappropriate signals.

data.title: 2.2.2.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
2.2.2.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define impulse propagation and explain its role in cardiac electrophysiology.

●       Describe how electrical impulses travel from one cardiac cell to another.

●       Understand the mechanisms of cell-to-cell conduction and gap junction function.

●       Explain the concept of conduction velocity and why it varies in different cardiac tissues.

●       Recognize the importance of impulse propagation in maintaining synchronized heart rhythm.

●       Relate abnormalities in impulse propagation to arrhythmias and device therapy.

2.2.2.H2 Explanation

2.2.2.C2 Impulse propagation refers to the movement of electrical impulses through the heart’s conduction system and myocardial tissue. Once an electrical impulse is generated—typically by the SA node—it must travel rapidly and efficiently through cardiac tissue to stimulate the atria and ventricles in a coordinated manner. This organized spread of electrical activity allows the heart to contract sequentially and pump blood effectively.

Without proper impulse propagation:

●       Cardiac contraction becomes uncoordinated

●       Blood flow becomes inefficient

●       Arrhythmias may develop

●       Cardiac output decreases

Impulse propagation is one of the most important processes in cardiac electrophysiology because it links electrical impulse generation with mechanical pumping.

Subtopic 1: How Electrical Impulses Travel Through the Heart

Cardiac muscle cells are electrically connected to each other, allowing impulses to spread from one cell to the next.

When one cardiac cell depolarizes:

●       Positive ions enter the cell

●       This changes the electrical charge of that cell

●       Adjacent cells detect this change

●       Electrical current spreads to neighboring cells

●       Neighboring cells depolarize in sequence

This process continues until the electrical impulse has spread through the heart.

Unlike nerve conduction, where impulses travel along isolated nerve fibers, cardiac conduction spreads:

Cell-to-cell through interconnected myocardial tissue

Subtopic 2: Role of Gap Junctions

Cardiac cells are connected by specialized structures called gap junctions.

Gap junctions are:

●       Tiny channels between adjacent cardiac cells

●       Located in intercalated discs

●       Allow ions and electrical current to pass directly between cells

Function of gap junctions:

●       Facilitate rapid electrical communication

●       Allow myocardium to function as a single unit

Because of gap junctions:

The heart behaves like a functional syncytium, meaning many cells contract together as one coordinated muscle.

Without gap junctions:

●       Electrical conduction would be interrupted

●       Myocardial contraction would be disorganized

Subtopic 3: Functional Syncytium

A syncytium refers to a group of cells that function together as a coordinated unit.

The heart has two major syncytia:

Atrial Syncytium

Includes:

●       Right and left atrial myocardium

Ventricular Syncytium

Includes:

●       Right and left ventricular myocardium

These are separated electrically by the fibrous cardiac skeleton, meaning:

●       Impulses cannot travel directly from atria to ventricles

●       They must pass through the AV node and Bundle of His

Subtopic 4: Conduction Velocity

Conduction velocity refers to the speed at which electrical impulses travel through cardiac tissue.

Different cardiac tissues conduct at different speeds:

Tissue

Approximate Velocity

SA Node

Slow

AV Node

Very Slow

Atrial Muscle

Moderate

Bundle Branches

Fast

Purkinje Fibers

Very Fast

Subtopic 5: Why Conduction Speed Varies

Different conduction speeds serve different purposes.

Slow Conduction in AV Node

Purpose:

●       Creates AV delay

●       Allows ventricular filling before contraction

Fast Conduction in Purkinje System

Purpose:

●       Enables synchronized ventricular activation

●       Ensures efficient contraction

Thus:

Conduction speed is physiologically optimized for heart efficiency.

Subtopic 6: Direction of Impulse Propagation

The normal direction of impulse propagation is:

1.    SA Node

2.    Atria

3.    AV Node

4.    Bundle of His

5.    Bundle Branches

6.    Purkinje Fibers

7.    Ventricular Myocardium

This organized sequence ensures:

●       Top-to-bottom activation

●       Sequential contraction

●       Efficient pumping

Subtopic 7: Conduction Through Myocardium vs Specialized Tissue

Impulse conduction differs between:

Specialized Conduction Tissue

Examples:

●       SA node

●       AV node

●       Purkinje system

Characteristics:

●       Fast, organized conduction

●       Designed for electrical transmission

 

Myocardial Tissue

Characteristics:

●       Slower conduction

●       Primarily contractile function

Subtopic 8: Abnormal Impulse Propagation

If impulse propagation is disrupted:

●       Conduction delays occur

●       Blocks may develop

●       Arrhythmias may result

Causes include:

●       Ischemia

●       Scar tissue

●       Fibrosis

●       Electrolyte imbalance

●       Structural heart disease

Subtopic 9: Reentry and Abnormal Propagation

Abnormal propagation may lead to:

Reentry Circuits

Reentry occurs when:

●       Electrical impulse re-circulates abnormally

●       Continuously reactivates myocardium

Can cause:

●       SVT

●       VT

●       AF

This is one of the most common mechanisms of arrhythmia.

Subtopic 10: Impulse Propagation and Device Therapy

Cardiac devices depend heavily on understanding propagation.

Pacemakers

Deliver impulse to initiate propagation.

CRT Devices

Correct abnormal ventricular propagation.

ICDs

Detects abnormal conduction/arrhythmias.

EP Mapping Systems

Analyze impulse propagation pathways.

data.title: 2.2.3.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
2.2.3.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define cardiac action potential and explain its importance in heart rhythm generation.

●       Describe the phases of the cardiac action potential in myocardial cells.

●       Understand the role of sodium, potassium, and calcium ions in cardiac electrophysiology.

●       Differentiate between fast-response and slow-response action potentials.

●       Explain how action potentials relate to depolarization, repolarization, and refractory periods.

●       Recognize the clinical and device relevance of action potential abnormalities in arrhythmias and pacing therapy.

 

 

2.2.3.H2 Explanation

2.2.3.C1 The cardiac action potential is the electrical event that occurs when a cardiac cell becomes activated and then returns to its resting state. It represents the rapid changes in membrane voltage that allow the heart to generate and conduct electrical impulses, ultimately leading to myocardial contraction.

Every heartbeat depends on action potentials occurring in millions of cardiac cells. Without action potentials:

●       Electrical impulses could not be generated

●       Myocardial contraction would not occur

●       Blood circulation would stop

An action potential is created when ions move across the cell membrane, changing the electrical charge of the cell. This process happens in a highly controlled sequence and is the basis of all cardiac electrical activity.

To understand action potentials, remember:

●       Resting cardiac cells are negatively charged inside

●       When stimulated, ion movement changes this charge

●       This creates electrical activation

●       The cell then resets for the next beat

The complete action potential consists of five phases, labeled Phase 0 through Phase 4.

Subtopic 1: Resting State – Phase 4

Phase 4 is the resting phase of the cardiac cell.

During this phase:

●       The cell is fully polarized

●       Inside of cell is negatively charged

●       Membrane potential is approximately –90 mV

Ion distribution:

●       Potassium high inside cell

●       Sodium high outside cell

●       Calcium high outside cell

Purpose of Phase 4:

●       Prepares cell for next electrical stimulus

●       Maintains resting membrane potential

Pacemaker cells are different because:

●       They do not stay stable in Phase 4

●       They gradually depolarize automatically

Subtopic 2: Rapid Depolarization – Phase 0

Phase 0 is the rapid depolarization phase.

Occurs when:

●       Threshold is reached

●       Fast sodium channels open

●       Sodium rushes into the cell

Result:

●       Inside of cell becomes positive rapidly

●       Membrane potential rises sharply

This phase produces:

●       Electrical activation

●       Initiation of contraction

Phase 0 determines:

●       Speed of impulse conduction through myocardium

Fast Phase 0 = Fast conduction.

Subtopic 3: Initial Repolarization – Phase 1

Phase 1 is the brief early repolarization phase.

Occurs when:

●       Sodium channels close

●       Small amount of potassium exits

Result:

●       Slight drop in membrane potential

This is a short transitional phase before plateau.

Subtopic 4: Plateau Phase – Phase 2

Phase 2 is the plateau phase.

This phase is unique to cardiac muscle and critical for sustained contraction.

Occurs when:

●       Calcium enters cell slowly

●       Potassium exits simultaneously

Balance between:

●       Positive calcium influx

●       Positive potassium efflux

Creates:

●       Stable plateau in membrane potential

Purpose:

●       Prolong contraction

●       Prevent tetanic contraction

●       Ensure coordinated pump function

This phase allows:

Sustained ventricular contraction long enough for blood ejection.

Subtopic 5: Repolarization – Phase 3

Phase 3 is final repolarization.

Occurs when:

●       Calcium channels close

●       Potassium exits rapidly

Result:

●       Cell returns to negative resting charge

This restores:

●       Polarized state

●       Readiness for next impulse

Subtopic 6: Fast vs Slow Response Action Potentials

There are two main types of cardiac action potentials.

Fast Response Action Potentials

Seen in:

●       Atrial myocardium

●       Ventricular myocardium

●       Purkinje fibers

Characteristics:

●       Rapid Phase 0

●       Sodium-dependent depolarization

Purpose:

●       Rapid conduction

Slow Response Action Potentials

Seen in:

●       SA node

●       AV node

Characteristics:

●       Slow depolarization

●       Calcium-dependent

Purpose:

●       Pacemaker activity

Subtopic 7: Automaticity in Pacemaker Cells

Pacemaker cells differ because:

They spontaneously depolarize during Phase 4.

Mechanism:

●       Slow sodium leak inward

●       Calcium entry

●       Gradual depolarization

This creates:

Automatic rhythm generation.

Seen in:

●       SA node

●       AV node

Subtopic 8: Refractory Periods

After depolarization:
Cells require time before firing again.

This is called:

Refractory Period

Subtopic 9: Why Action Potential Matters Clinically

Action potential abnormalities can cause:

●       Bradycardia

●       Tachycardia

●       Reentry arrhythmias

●       QT prolongation

●       Sudden cardiac death

Drugs often affect action potential phases:

●       Antiarrhythmics alter ion channels

●       Electrolyte abnormalities change action potential

Subtopic 10: Action Potential and Device Therapy

Understanding action potential is critical for:

Pacemakers

Deliver stimulus to trigger Phase 0 depolarization.

ICDs

Detect abnormal action potentials.

EP Studies

Map abnormal electrical activation.

Defibrillation

Resets disorganized action potentials.

data.title: 2.2.4.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
2.2.4.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define refractory period and explain its role in cardiac electrophysiology.

●       Differentiate between absolute refractory period, relative refractory period, and effective refractory period.

●       Explain the concept of cardiac excitability and myocardial responsiveness to electrical stimulation.

●       Understand how refractory periods prevent abnormal repetitive contraction and arrhythmias.

●       Relate refractory period concepts to pacing, sensing, ICD therapy, and arrhythmia mechanisms.

●       Apply refractory period knowledge in device programming and troubleshooting.

2.2.4.H2 Explanation

2.2.4.C2 The heart is designed to contract in a rhythmic, organized pattern. After each electrical impulse and contraction, the cardiac cells need time to recover before they can respond to another electrical stimulus. This recovery time is known as the refractory period.

The refractory period is one of the most important protective mechanisms in cardiac electrophysiology because it prevents the heart from being stimulated continuously or contracting in an uncontrolled manner. Without refractory periods, the myocardium could respond to repeated rapid impulses without relaxation, leading to ineffective pumping and life-threatening arrhythmias.

Closely related to the refractory period is the concept of excitability, which refers to the ability of cardiac cells to respond to an electrical stimulus and generate an action potential. Excitability changes throughout the cardiac cycle depending on whether the cell is in a refractory or recovered state.

Understanding refractory periods and excitability is essential in cardiac rhythm management because pacemakers, ICDs, and electrophysiology studies all rely heavily on these principles for sensing, pacing, and arrhythmia detection.

Subtopic 1: What Is a Refractory Period?

A refractory period is the period of time after a cardiac cell has depolarized during which it is unable or less able to respond to another electrical stimulus.

In simple terms:

After a heart cell fires, it must “reset” before it can fire again.

Purpose:

●       Allows proper recovery of ion channels

●       Prevents repeated immediate stimulation

●       Ensures organized rhythmic contraction

Without refractory periods:

●       Cardiac cells could fire continuously

●       Heart would lose pumping efficiency

Subtopic 2: Why Refractory Periods Are Necessary

Refractory periods serve several critical functions:

Prevent Tetanic Contraction

Unlike skeletal muscle, the heart cannot remain continuously contracted.

Maintain Rhythmic Pumping

Allows relaxation between beats.

Prevent Premature Reactivation

Stops one impulse from immediately retriggering the myocardium.

Protect Against Dangerous Arrhythmias

Reduces likelihood of uncontrolled repetitive firing.

Thus:

Refractory periods are essential for normal heart rhythm and survival.

Subtopic 3: Absolute Refractory Period (ARP)

The Absolute Refractory Period is the period during which no new electrical stimulus—no matter how strong—can trigger another action potential.

Occurs because:

●       Sodium channels are inactivated

●       Cell cannot depolarize again

Timing:

●       Begins during depolarization

●       Continues through most of repolarization

Clinical Importance:

●       Prevents immediate reactivation of myocardium

●       Maintains one contraction per beat

Subtopic 4: Relative Refractory Period (RRP)

The Relative Refractory Period occurs after the absolute refractory period.

During this phase:

●       Some ion channels recover

●       A stronger-than-normal stimulus may trigger depolarization

Characteristics:

●       Cell is partially excitable

●       Response threshold is elevated

Clinical Significance:

●       Premature beats may occur here

●       Vulnerable period for arrhythmia initiation

Subtopic 5: Effective Refractory Period (ERP)

The Effective Refractory Period is the time during which a stimulus may depolarize the cell locally but cannot generate a propagated response.

This means:

●       Electrical activity may begin

●       But cannot spread effectively to neighboring cells

Importance:

●       Critical in arrhythmia prevention

●       Used in EP studies and antiarrhythmic drug evaluation

Subtopic 6: Vulnerable Period

A particularly dangerous time occurs late in repolarization:

Vulnerable Period

This is when:

●       Some cells are recovered

●       Others remain refractory

If a premature impulse occurs here:

●       Dangerous arrhythmias may develop

Examples:

●       Ventricular tachycardia

●       Ventricular fibrillation

This corresponds to:

Peak/downslope of T wave on ECG

Subtopic 7: What Is Excitability?

Excitability is the ability of cardiac cells to respond to an electrical stimulus.

For a cell to be excitable:

●       Membrane must be recovered

●       Ion channels must be functional

●       Stimulus must exceed threshold

Excitability varies depending on:

●       Phase of action potential

●       Refractory status

●       Electrolyte balance

Subtopic 8: Factors Affecting Excitability

Excitability may increase or decrease based on:

Electrolyte Imbalance

●       Hyperkalemia

●       Hypokalemia

Ischemia

Damaged myocardium less excitable.

Medications

Antiarrhythmics alter excitability.

Scar Tissue

Reduces response capability.

Fibrosis

Disrupts electrical responsiveness.

Subtopic 9: Refractory Period and Arrhythmias

Abnormal refractory periods contribute to arrhythmia development.

Too short:

●       Allows rapid reactivation

●       Promotes tachyarrhythmias

Too long:

●       Causes conduction delay

●       May predispose to torsades/QT issues

Uneven refractory periods:

●       Promote reentry circuits

 

Subtopic 10: Device Relevance of Refractory Periods

Refractory periods are crucial in device programming.

Pacemaker Refractory Periods

Prevent oversensing of:

●       T waves

●       Retrograde P waves

●       Noise

ICD Detection Algorithms

Analyze refractory timing during tachyarrhythmias.

EP Studies

Measure refractory periods for arrhythmia assessment.

ATP Therapy

Times pacing based on refractory periods.

Subtopic 11: Pacemaker Refractory Programming

Pacemakers include programmable refractory periods:

Examples:

●       Post-Ventricular Atrial Refractory Period (PVARP)

●       Ventricular Refractory Period (VRP)

Purpose:

●       Prevent inappropriate sensing

●       Avoid pacemaker-mediated tachycardia

data.title: 3.1.1.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.1.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define an electrocardiogram (ECG).

●       Explain how ECG signals are generated.

●       Understand what an ECG measures and what it does not measure.

●       Identify common clinical uses of ECG.

●       Recognize why ECG interpretation is essential in pacemaker therapy.

 

3.1.1.H2 Explanation

3.1.1.C2 An electrocardiogram (ECG), also written as EKG, is a graphic recording of the heart’s electrical activity detected from the body surface using skin electrodes. It is one of the most widely used diagnostic tools in medicine because it is fast, non-invasive, inexpensive, and highly valuable in assessing rhythm and conduction abnormalities.

In simple terms:

ECG = A tracing that shows how electrical impulses move through the heart.

Every heartbeat begins with an electrical signal. This signal starts in the sinoatrial (SA) node, spreads through the atria, pauses briefly in the atrioventricular (AV) node, then travels through the His-Purkinje system to activate the ventricles. As this wave of electrical activation moves through the myocardium, it creates small voltage differences that can be detected by electrodes placed on the skin.

These signals are amplified and displayed as waveforms on ECG paper or a digital screen.

Why the Heart Produces Electrical Signals

The heart is a specialized muscular organ that contracts rhythmically. For contraction to occur in an organized way, the muscle cells must be activated electrically in the correct sequence.

Normal sequence:

SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → right/left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricles

This coordinated activation ensures:

●       Atria contract first to fill ventricles

●       Ventricles contract next to pump blood out

●       Heart rate adapts to body needs

What an ECG Measures

The ECG records electrical timing and direction, not direct mechanical pumping force.

It helps evaluate:

1. Heart Rate

●       Bradycardia (slow)

●       Normal rate

●       Tachycardia (fast)

2. Rhythm

●       Sinus rhythm

●       Atrial fibrillation

●       Flutter

●       Paced rhythm

●       Ventricular arrhythmias

3. Conduction

●       AV block

●       Bundle branch block

●       Pre-excitation

●       Delayed intraventricular conduction

4. Chamber Activation Patterns

May suggest hypertrophy or enlargement.

5. Ischemia / Injury Clues

ST segment and T wave changes may indicate acute or chronic coronary syndromes.

6. Pacemaker Performance

●       Pacing spikes

●       Capture

●       Sensing issues

●       Mode behavior clues

What an ECG Does NOT Measure Directly

An ECG does not directly tell you:

●       Ejection fraction

●       Valve anatomy

●       Chamber pressures

●       Coronary blockage severity alone

●       Exact stroke volume

●       Mechanical contractile strength

These require other tools such as echocardiography, imaging, or catheterization.

Electrical vs Mechanical Function

The ECG may show organized electrical rhythm, but the patient may still have poor circulation (e.g., shock or pulseless electrical activity).

Therefore:

Good ECG rhythm ≠ always good circulation.

Always correlate ECG with:

●       Symptoms

●       Pulse

●       Blood pressure

●       Oxygenation

data.title: 3.1.2.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.1.2.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Describe the structure of ECG paper and grid lines.

●       Analysing an ECG strip for Rhythm diseases

●       Calculate heart rate and intervals from ECG strip.

●       Apply these principles to rhythm diagnosis and pacemaker analysis.

3.1.2.H2 Explanation

3.1.2.C2 The ECG tracing is displayed on a standardized graph paper or digital grid that allows clinicians to measure time, voltage, and rhythm intervals accurately. Understanding ECG paper is one of the first practical skills in ECG interpretation.

In simple terms:

ECG paper = A ruler for heart electricity.

Without knowing paper speed and calibration, even experienced users can misinterpret:

●       Heart rate

●       PR interval

●       QRS duration

●       QT interval

●       Pacemaker timing

●       Rhythm regularity

This topic is especially important for cardiac device specialists because pacing cycles, AV delays, escape rhythms, and sensing behavior often require precise measurement.

Basic Layout of ECG Paper

The ECG grid has:

●       Small boxes

●       Large boxes (5 small boxes together)

●       Horizontal axis = time

●       Vertical axis = voltage/amplitude

The grid may be printed red or gray, but the scale remains standardized.

Horizontal Axis = Time

At the standard ECG recording speed of 25 mm/sec:

One Small Box

= 0.04 seconds
= 40 milliseconds

One Large Box (5 small boxes)

= 0.20 seconds
= 200 milliseconds

Five Large Boxes

= 1 second

This is the basis for measuring intervals and heart rate.

 

 

Measuring Heart Rate

Heart Rate refers to Ventricular Rate is the number of heartbeats or R-R cycles that occur in one minute

e.g. if 60 R-R cycles occur in a minute, Rate=60bpm

 

•The period of each R-R Cycle is called an R-R interval and its duration is specified in milliseconds

•There are 60 X 1000 milliseconds in a minute

•Rate = No. of R-R cycles in 60000 ms

•Rate = 60000/duration of each R-R cycle in ms

 

Method 1: Small Box Method

HR=1500small boxes between R wavesHR = \frac{1500}{\text{small boxes between R waves}}HR=small boxes between R waves1500​

More precise for regular rhythms.

Example

R-R Interval = 5 boxes = 5 X 200 ms = 1000ms

Rate = 60000/R-R Interval = 60000/1000 = 60 bpm

 

 

Method 2: Large Box Method (Regular Rhythm)

HR=300large boxes between R wavesHR = \frac{300}{\text{large boxes between R waves}}HR=large boxes between R waves300​

Examples:

 

Method 3: 6-Second Method (Irregular Rhythm)

Count QRS complexes in 30 large boxes (6 seconds), then multiply by 10.

Useful in atrial fibrillation.

 

 

Measuring Common Intervals

PR Interval

Start of P wave to start of QRS.

Normal:

●       120–200 ms

●       3 to 5 small boxes

QRS Duration

Beginning to end of QRS.

Usually:

●       <120 ms

QT Interval

Start of QRS to end of T wave.

Must be corrected for heart rate (QTc).

Heart Rate measurement exercises

 

 

3.1.2.H3 Pacemaker Relevance

3.1.2.C3 Accurate grid interpretation helps identify:

●       Programmed lower pacing rate

●       AV delay timing

●       Atrial paced to ventricular paced intervals

●       Failure to capture

●       Undersensing pauses

●       Oversensing inhibition

●       Fusion beats

Common Beginner Errors

Error 1: Counting Wrong Boxes

Confusing small with large boxes.

Error 2: Ignoring Speed

Intervals misread if speed unknown.

Error 3: Ignoring Gain

Low voltage may be machine setting, not pathology.

Error 4: Measuring from Peak Instead of Onset

Use waveform start/end, not tallest point.

Digital Monitors

Modern ECG monitors may use digital display instead of paper, but the same principles apply:

●       Sweep speed

●       Gain

●       Grid scale

Practical Tip for Device Specialists

When evaluating pacing spikes:

●       Increase sweep speed if available

●       Use multiple leads

●       Zoom digital strips when possible

Memory Aid

Horizontal = Time

Vertical = Voltage

25 mm/sec = Standard

10 mm = 1 mV

data.title: 3.2.1.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.2.1.C1 By the end of this section, learners will be able to:

●       Identify all major ECG components in one heartbeat.

●       Explain what each waveform, segment, and interval represents.

●       Relate ECG components to cardiac conduction physiology.

●       Recognize why component analysis is essential in rhythm and pacemaker interpretation.

●       Prepare for detailed subtopics that follow.

3.2.1.H2 Explanation

3.2.1.C2 Every heartbeat recorded on an ECG is made of distinct parts called components. These include waves, segments, and intervals that represent specific electrical events occurring in the atria, AV node, ventricles, and recovery phase.

In simple terms:

ECG components are the alphabet of ECG interpretation.

If learners understand each component individually, they can later interpret:

●       Bradycardia

●       Tachycardia

●       AV block

●       Bundle branch block

●       Ischemia patterns

●       Pacemaker rhythms

●       Drug effects

●       Electrolyte abnormalities

A normal heartbeat commonly follows this sequence:

P wave → PR interval → QRS complex → ST segment → T wave → QT interval

Sometimes a U wave may also be seen.

Main ECG Components Overview

1. P Wave

Represents atrial depolarization.

Meaning:

●       Electrical activation of right and left atria

●       Usually first visible wave in normal sinus rhythm

Clinical relevance:

●       Identifies sinus rhythm

●       Detects atrial enlargement

●       Helps diagnose AF/flutter

●       Important for atrial sensing/pacing

2. PR Interval

Measured from start of P wave to start of QRS.

Represents:

●       Atrial depolarization + AV nodal conduction delay + His conduction time

Normal approx:

●       120–200 ms

Clinical relevance:

●       Long PR = first-degree AV block

●       Variable PR = Wenckebach possibility

●       Short PR = pre-excitation possibility

3. QRS Complex

Represents ventricular depolarization.

Usually largest waveform.

Normal width:

●       Typically <120 ms

Clinical relevance:

●       Wide QRS = BBB / ventricular origin / pacing

●       Narrow QRS = supraventricular conduction usually

4. ST Segment

Begins at end of QRS (J point) and ends at start of T wave.

Represents early ventricular recovery phase.

Normally near baseline.

Clinical relevance:

●       ST elevation may suggest acute injury pattern

●       ST depression may suggest ischemia or demand mismatch

5. T Wave

Represents ventricular repolarization.

Usually upright in many leads.

Clinical relevance:

●       Inversion may indicate ischemia or strain

●       Tall peaked T may suggest hyperkalemia

6. QT Interval

Measured from start of QRS to end of T wave.

Represents total ventricular electrical activation + recovery.

Changes with heart rate.

Clinical relevance:

●       Long QT increases risk of dangerous arrhythmia

●       Drug safety monitoring important

7. U Wave (Occasional)

Small wave after T wave.

May be normal or more visible in:

●       Bradycardia

●       Hypokalemia

Waves vs Segments vs Intervals

Waves

Visible deflections.

Examples:

●       P

●       QRS

●       T

Segments

Flat portions between waves.

Examples:

●       PR segment

●       ST segment

Intervals

Include waves + segments.

Examples:

●       PR interval

●       QT interval

Why ECG Components Matter in Pacemaker Patients

P Wave

Needed for atrial sensing.

PR Interval

Relevant to AV synchrony.

QRS

Used to assess ventricular pacing morphology.

ST/T

Can be altered after pacing; interpret carefully.

QT

May be relevant in drugs and bradycardia patients.

 

Quick Memory Sequence

P → PR → QRS → ST → T → QT

Think:

●       Atria start

●       Delay

●       Ventricles activate

●       Plateau

●       Recover

●       Total ventricular time

Common Beginner Errors

●       Confusing PR interval with PR segment

●       Calling T wave a P wave

●       Missing wide paced QRS

●       Measuring QT incorrectly

●       Ignoring hidden P waves

data.title: 3.3.1.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.3.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define the P wave and explain how it is generated.

●       Identify normal P-wave characteristics.

●       Recognize common abnormal P-wave patterns.

●       Use P-wave analysis for rhythm diagnosis.

●       Apply P-wave concepts in pacemaker patients.

3.3.1.H2 Explanation

3.3.1.C2 The P wave is the ECG waveform that represents atrial depolarization—the electrical activation of the right and left atria before they contract.

In simple terms:

P wave = The signal that tells the atria to beat.

It is usually the first visible component of a normal heartbeat and provides important information about where the rhythm starts and how atrial activation is occurring.

For beginners, the P wave is one of the most valuable rhythm clues. For cardiac device professionals, it is essential because many pacemakers sense or pace the atria.

How the P Wave Is Generated

Normal atrial activation begins in the sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the upper right atrium near the superior vena cava.

The impulse spreads in sequence:

1.    Through the right atrium

2.    Across interatrial conduction pathways (including Bachmann’s bundle)

3.    Into the left atrium

4.    Toward the AV node

This coordinated electrical movement creates the surface P wave seen on ECG.

Because the right atrium activates slightly before the left atrium, the P wave reflects the combined depolarization of both atria.

Why the P Wave Matters

P-wave analysis helps determine:

●       Is rhythm sinus or non-sinus?

●       Is atrial activity present?

●       Is there AV association with QRS?

●       Is atrial enlargement possible?

●       Is atrial pacing occurring?

●       Is atrial fibrillation/flutter present?

Normal P-Wave Characteristics

In normal sinus rhythm, the P wave is commonly:

●       Present before each QRS complex

●       Uniform in shape beat-to-beat

●       Upright in Lead II

●       Upright in Leads I and aVF (commonly)

●       Negative in aVR

●       Smooth and rounded

●       Duration usually <120 ms

●       Amplitude often <2.5 mm in inferior leads

Best Leads to Assess the P Wave

Lead II

Often the clearest lead for P-wave visibility.

V1

Helpful for biphasic P-wave analysis and atrial abnormality clues.

aVR

Normally negative P wave in sinus rhythm.

P Wave and Sinus Rhythm

A rhythm is likely sinus when:

●       P wave before every QRS

●       Each P followed by QRS

●       Stable PR interval

●       Consistent P-wave morphology

●       Expected axis (upright in II, negative in aVR)

Abnormal P-Wave Patterns

1. No Visible P Waves

May occur in:

●       Atrial fibrillation

●       Junctional rhythm

●       Hidden P waves in tachycardia

●       Artifact obscuring signal

2. Inverted P Waves

May suggest:

●       Low atrial rhythm

●       Junctional rhythm

●       Retrograde atrial activation

If P waves are inverted in Lead II, think non-sinus origin.

3. Tall Peaked P Waves

May suggest right atrial enlargement.

Historically called P pulmonale.

Possible causes:

●       Pulmonary hypertension

●       COPD

●       Tricuspid disease

4. Broad / Notched P Waves

May suggest left atrial abnormality.

Historically called P mitrale.

Possible causes:

●       Mitral valve disease

●       Hypertension

●       Diastolic dysfunction

5. Changing P-Wave Shape

May suggest:

●       Wandering atrial pacemaker

●       Multifocal atrial rhythm

Different atrial foci produce different morphologies.

Hidden or Difficult P Waves

P waves may be concealed:

●       Inside preceding T wave

●       Within QRS complex

●       During rapid SVT

●       During ventricular pacing

Use multiple leads and slower sweep speed if available.

P Wave Relationship to PR Interval

The P wave marks atrial depolarization, but the PR interval includes:

●       P-wave duration

●       AV nodal delay

●       His conduction time

Thus P wave alone does not assess AV conduction fully.

P Waves in Atrial Arrhythmias

Atrial Fibrillation

No organized P waves. Chaotic baseline.

Atrial Flutter

Sawtooth flutter waves instead of normal P waves.

Atrial Tachycardia

Abnormal but organized atrial waves.

Pacemaker Relevance

Atrial Sensing

Pacemaker detects intrinsic P waves.

Atrial Pacing

Pacing spike before atrial depolarization.

Dual-Chamber Tracking

P waves may trigger ventricular pacing after AV delay in tracking modes.

Atrial Undersensing

Intrinsic P waves missed.

Oversensing

Noise mistaken as atrial activity.

Clinical Examples

Example 1

Rate 52 bpm, upright P before every QRS
→ Likely sinus bradycardia

Example 2

Irregular rhythm, no organized P waves
→ Likely atrial fibrillation

Example 3

Spike before P wave, then QRS later
→ Atrial paced rhythm

Common Beginner Errors

●       Calling every baseline bump a P wave

●       Ignoring Lead II

●       Diagnosing AF without checking artifact

●       Missing retrograde P waves

●       Forgetting P-QRS relationship

Practical 5-Step P-Wave Check

1.    Is a P wave present?

2.    Is it before each QRS?

3.    Is morphology consistent?

4.    Upright in Lead II?

5.    Is PR relationship logical?

Memory Aid

P = Precedes QRS in sinus rhythm

P = Atrial Pacemaker clue

data.title: 3.4.1.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.4.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define the QRS complex and explain what it represents.

●       Identify normal QRS morphology and duration.

●       Differentiate narrow vs wide QRS complexes.

●       Recognize common causes of abnormal QRS patterns.

●       Apply QRS analysis in pacemaker patients.

3.4.1.H2 Explanation

3.4.1.C2 The QRS complex is the ECG waveform that represents ventricular depolarization, meaning the electrical activation of the right and left ventricles before they contract.

In simple terms:

QRS = Signal telling the ventricles to pump.

Because the ventricles are larger muscle chambers than the atria, the QRS complex is usually the largest and most prominent waveform on the ECG.

It is one of the most clinically valuable ECG components because it helps assess:

●       Ventricular conduction speed

●       Origin of rhythm

●       Bundle branch blocks

●       Ventricular arrhythmias

●       Pacemaker capture

●       Chamber activation synchrony

How the QRS Complex Is Generated

After the impulse passes through the AV node, it travels rapidly through:

1.    His bundle

2.    Right bundle branch

3.    Left bundle branch

4.    Purkinje network

5.    Ventricular myocardium

Rapid organized activation produces a relatively narrow QRS in healthy conduction systems.

Components of the QRS Complex

Q Wave

First negative deflection before any positive wave.

R Wave

First positive deflection.

S Wave

Negative deflection after an R wave.

Not every QRS contains all three parts.

Examples:

●       R only

●       RS

●       qR

●       rSr'

●       QS

Normal QRS Duration

At standard ECG speed:

Normal:

QRS<120 msQRS < 120\text{ ms}QRS<120 ms

Equivalent:

●       Less than 3 small boxes

A narrow QRS usually means ventricular activation is using the normal His-Purkinje system.

Why QRS Width Matters

Narrow QRS

Usually indicates:

●       Supraventricular origin with normal ventricular conduction

●       Sinus rhythm

●       Atrial fibrillation with intact conduction

●       SVT (often narrow)

Wide QRS

May indicate:

●       Bundle branch block

●       Ventricular rhythm

●       Ventricular pacing

●       Hyperkalemia

●       Pre-excitation

●       Nonspecific intraventricular delay

QRS Morphology Basics

The shape of the QRS depends on:

●       Lead viewed

●       Conduction pathway used

●       Ventricular origin of beat

●       Presence of scar

●       Pacing site

Thus the same beat looks different in V1 vs V6.

R-Wave Progression (Chest Leads)

Normally across V1 to V6:

●       Small R in V1

●       Increasing R through V3/V4

●       Larger R in V5/V6

Poor progression may occur in:

●       Prior anterior MI

●       Lead misplacement

●       LVH

●       RV pacing

Pathologic Q Waves

Deep or wide Q waves in certain leads may suggest prior myocardial infarction or scar.

Clinical correlation required.

Common Wide QRS Causes

1. Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB)

Delayed RV activation.

Often rsR' in V1.

2. Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)

Delayed LV activation.

Broad QRS with characteristic lateral changes.

3. Ventricular Tachycardia

Wide-complex tachycardia often presumed VT until proven otherwise.

4. Ventricular Pacing

Pacing spike followed by wide QRS.

 

Pacemaker Relevance

Ventricular Capture

Spike followed by wide QRS indicates paced depolarization.

RV Apical Pacing

Often creates LBBB-like morphology.

CRT / Biventricular Pacing

May narrow QRS compared with intrinsic LBBB.

Loss of Capture

Spike without resulting QRS.

Fusion Beats

Part intrinsic, part paced QRS.

QRS in Tachycardia Interpretation

When fast rhythm occurs:

Narrow Complex Tachycardia

Usually supraventricular.

Wide Complex Tachycardia

Could be:

●       VT

●       SVT with aberrancy

●       Paced rhythm

Clinical caution required.

Common Beginner Errors

●       Thinking all wide QRS = VT

●       Missing pacing spike before wide QRS

●       Measuring from peak instead of onset/offset

●       Ignoring lead placement artifact

●       Calling BBB based on one lead only

Practical QRS Review Method

Ask:

1.    Is QRS narrow or wide?

2.    Is rhythm fast or slow?

3.    Is pacing spike present?

4.    Is morphology consistent?

5.    Is this new vs old ECG?

Clinical Examples

Example 1

Sinus rhythm, QRS 90 ms
→ Normal narrow complex conduction

Example 2

Rate 160, wide regular QRS
→ Treat as VT until proven otherwise

 

Example 3

Pacing spike then wide QRS
→ Ventricular pacing capture

Example 4

Intrinsic LBBB, CRT pacing narrows QRS
→ Improved synchrony clue

Memory Aid

P = Atria

QRS = Ventricles

Wide = Slow/Abnormal pathway

Visual Hint

data.title: 3.5.1.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.5.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define the T wave and explain what it represents.

●       Identify normal T-wave morphology.

●       Recognize common abnormal T-wave patterns.

●       Understand clinical causes of T-wave changes.

●       Apply T-wave interpretation in paced rhythms and device patients.

3.5.1.H2 Explanation

3.5.1.C2 The T wave is the ECG waveform that represents ventricular repolarization, meaning the electrical recovery of ventricular muscle cells after depolarization and contraction.

In simple terms:

T wave = The ventricles resetting for the next beat.

After the QRS complex activates the ventricles, the ventricular myocardium must recover electrically before the next heartbeat can occur. This recovery process generates the T wave.

Although often less dramatic than the QRS complex, the T wave can provide major clues regarding:

●       Ischemia

●       Electrolyte abnormalities

●       Drug effects

●       Conduction abnormalities

●       CNS stress responses

●       Secondary changes after pacing or bundle branch block

Why the T Wave Appears Upright in Many Leads

Depolarization and repolarization move through the ventricles differently. Because of these electrical properties, the T wave is often upright in many leads where the QRS is upright.

This is normal physiology.

Normal T-Wave Characteristics

A normal T wave is commonly:

●       Smooth and asymmetric

●       Rounded contour

●       Concordant with QRS in many leads (same general direction)

●       Upright in Leads I, II, V3–V6 commonly

●       Variable in V1

●       Negative in aVR commonly

Amplitude varies by lead and individual.

Why T Waves Matter Clinically

T-wave abnormalities may be early or subtle markers of disease. They can reflect disturbances in repolarization caused by:

●       Reduced blood flow

●       Electrolyte imbalance

●       Structural heart disease

●       Medications

●       Wide QRS conduction patterns

Common Abnormal T-Wave Patterns

1. T-Wave Inversion

The T wave becomes negative in leads where upright is expected.

Possible causes:

●       Ischemia

●       Prior infarction changes

●       Ventricular strain

●       CNS events

●       Post-tachycardia memory changes

●       Bundle branch block / pacing secondary changes

2. Tall Peaked T Waves

Narrow, tented, prominent T waves may suggest:

●       Hyperkalemia

This can be clinically urgent.

3. Flat T Waves

Low-amplitude T waves may be seen with:

●       Hypokalemia

●       Nonspecific changes

●       Medications

●       Ischemia

4. Biphasic T Waves

Part positive and part negative.

May occur in:

●       Ischemia patterns

●       Electrolyte disorders

●       Nonspecific repolarization changes

5. Hyperacute T Waves

Broad, large T waves may appear early in acute coronary occlusion before obvious ST elevation.

Clinical context important.

T-Wave Changes in Ischemia

T-wave abnormalities may precede or accompany ST changes.

Examples:

●       Symmetric inversion

●       Hyperacute broad T waves

●       Dynamic changes over time

Serial ECG comparison is valuable.

T Waves and Electrolytes

Hyperkalemia

●       Tall peaked T waves

●       Widening QRS later if severe

Hypokalemia

●       Flattened T waves

●       Prominent U waves

●       Arrhythmia risk

T Waves in Bundle Branch Block and Pacing

Wide QRS rhythms often produce secondary repolarization changes.

Example: RV Pacing

Wide paced QRS may show T wave opposite the major QRS direction.

Example: LBBB

Discordant ST-T patterns can be expected.

Therefore not every abnormal T wave means ischemia.

Pacemaker Relevance

Device professionals should know:

●       Ventricular pacing commonly alters T-wave appearance.

●       Compare paced ECG to prior paced ECG.

●       Sudden major new changes with symptoms require escalation.

●       Electrolyte disturbances can affect paced and intrinsic rhythms alike.

T-Wave Memory

After periods of pacing or tachycardia, T waves may remain altered temporarily even after normal conduction resumes. This is sometimes called cardiac memory.

Common Beginner Errors

●       Calling all inverted T waves ischemia

●       Ignoring pacing/BBB context

●       Missing hyperkalemic peaked T waves

●       Overreading isolated minor flattening

●       Ignoring dynamic changes over time

Practical T-Wave Review Method

Ask:

1.    Upright where expected?

2.    Peaked, flat, or inverted?

3.    Symmetric or nonspecific?

4.    Wide QRS / pacing present?

5.    Symptoms or electrolyte issue?

Clinical Examples

Example 1

Tall peaked T waves in multiple leads
→ Hyperkalemia concern

Example 2

New deep anterior T inversion + chest pain
→ Ischemic concern

Example 3

RV paced rhythm with discordant T waves
→ May be expected secondary change

Memory Aid

QRS = Activate

T = Recover

●       Dynamic T-wave changes are more important than static mild abnormalities.

●       Hyperkalemic peaked T waves may be urgent.

●       Pacing and LBBB often distort T waves.

●       Compare with previous ECGs.

●       Symptoms guide significance.

●       Isolated nonspecific flattening is common.

●       Electrolytes can strongly affect repolarization.

data.title: 3.6.1.H1 Learning Objective
data.content:
3.6.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.6.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to:

●       Define the PR interval and explain what it represents.

●       Measure the PR interval accurately on ECG.

●       Identify normal and abnormal PR intervals.

●       Recognize common conduction disorders involving the PR interval.

●       Apply PR interval concepts in pacemaker patients.

3.6.1.H2 Explanation

3.6.1.C2s The PR interval is the time measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex. It represents the time taken for the electrical impulse to travel from the atria to the ventricles.

In simple terms:

PR interval = Time from atrial activation to ventricular activation.

This includes:

●       Atrial depolarization

●       Conduction through the AV node

●       Delay in the AV node

●       His bundle conduction

●       Arrival of impulse to ventricular conduction system

The PR interval is one of the most clinically important ECG measurements because it reflects atrioventricular (AV) conduction.

Why the PR Interval Matters

The AV node normally slows conduction briefly. This delay allows:

●       Atria to contract first

●       Ventricles to fill adequately before systole

●       Efficient cardiac output

●       Coordinated timing between chambers

Without this delay, filling efficiency may decrease.

Where to Measure the PR Interval

Measure:

●       From the first visible deflection of the P wave

●       To the first deflection of the QRS complex

This could be:

●       Beginning of Q wave

●       Beginning of R wave if no Q wave present

Normal PR Interval

At standard speed (25 mm/sec):

Normal Range:

120 ms  to  200 ms120\text{ ms} \; to \; 200\text{ ms}120 msto200 ms

Equivalent to:

●       3 to 5 small boxes

What Happens Physiologically During the PR Interval?

The impulse travels through:

1.    SA node discharge (already occurred before P wave seen)

2.    Right and left atria

3.    AV node delay

4.    His bundle

5.    Bundle branches (early portion before QRS onset)

The AV node contributes the major delay.

Short PR Interval

A PR interval <120 ms may suggest:

1. Pre-excitation Syndrome

Example: accessory pathway conduction (e.g., WPW pattern).

2. Junctional Rhythm

Impulse starts near AV junction.

3. Ectopic Atrial Rhythm Near AV Node

Shorter distance to ventricles.

Prolonged PR Interval

PR interval >200 ms suggests delayed AV conduction.

Most common cause:

First-Degree AV Block

Every atrial impulse reaches ventricles, but slowly.

Example:

P before every QRS, but PR is long.

Progressive PR Changes

Second-Degree AV Block Type I (Wenckebach)

PR progressively lengthens until a QRS is dropped.

Variable PR with Conduction Disease

Can indicate more advanced pathology.

Fixed vs Changing PR Interval

Fixed PR Interval

Often sinus rhythm or first-degree AV block.

Changing PR Interval

May suggest:

●       AV block

●       Ectopic rhythms

●       AV dissociation

●       Pacemaker timing behavior

PR Interval in Bradycardia

A slow rate may mildly lengthen PR in some individuals, especially with increased vagal tone.

Seen in:

●       Athletes

●       Sleep

●       Young healthy adults

Clinical context matters.

PR Interval in Tachycardia

At faster heart rates, PR may shorten slightly due to autonomic changes, but persistent abnormalities still need evaluation.

Pacemaker Relevance

The PR interval is highly relevant in pacing therapy.

1. AV Synchrony

Proper atrial-to-ventricular timing improves filling.

2. Dual-Chamber Devices

Often track atrial activity and pace ventricles after programmed AV delay.

3. Long Native PR

Some symptomatic patients with very prolonged PR may lose hemodynamic efficiency.

4. Device Diagnostics

Surface ECG can help assess paced AV timing.

Clinical Symptoms of PR Problems

Many patients with isolated first-degree AV block are asymptomatic.

However, markedly prolonged PR may contribute to:

●       Fatigue

●       Reduced exercise tolerance

●       Palpitations

●       “Pseudo pacemaker syndrome” in some cases

Common Beginner Errors

●       Measuring from peak of P wave instead of start

●       Measuring to peak of R wave instead of QRS onset

●       Confusing PR interval with PR segment

●       Ignoring variable PR changes

●       Not checking paper speed

Practical Reading Method

Ask:

1.    Is there a P before every QRS?

2.    Is PR between 120–200 ms?

3.    Is PR fixed or changing?

4.    Any dropped beats?

5.    Is pacing involved?

Clinical Examples

Example 1

Regular rhythm, PR = 160 ms
→ Normal AV conduction

Example 2

PR = 260 ms, every P conducts
→ First-degree AV block

Example 3

Progressive PR prolongation then dropped QRS
→ Wenckebach pattern

Example 4

Atrial sensed event followed by paced QRS after delay
→ Dual-chamber pacing behavior

Memory Aid

P starts it

R receives it

PR = Travel time between them

data.title: 3.6.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions
data.content:
3.6.1.C3s

Term

Definition

PR Interval

Time from atrial activation to ventricular activation

AV Node

Electrical gateway between atria and ventricles

First-Degree AV Block

PR >200 ms with all beats conducted

Wenckebach

Progressive PR prolongation with dropped beat

AV Delay

Programmed paced atrial-to-ventricular timing

Clinical Pearl

●       PR interval reflects AV conduction, not just AV node alone.

●       First-degree AV block is often benign but context matters.

●       Markedly long PR can reduce AV synchrony.

●       Progressive PR prolongation suggests Wenckebach.

●       Short PR may indicate accessory pathway conduction.

●       Always measure from onset to onset.

●       Check PR in paced rhythms too.

●       Symptoms matter more than numbers alone.

data.title: Learning Objectives
data.content:
By the end of this chapter introduction, learners will be able to:

● Define cardiac arrhythmia in simple clinical terms.
● Explain how abnormal electrical impulse formation or conduction can disturb normal heartbeat rhythm.
● Differentiate between tachycardia and bradycardia based on heart rate.
● Recognize the main categories of cardiac arrhythmias.
● Explain why arrhythmias may reduce cardiac output.
● Identify common symptoms associated with abnormal heart rhythms.
● Understand why bradyarrhythmias are important in pacemaker and cardiac rhythm management practice.
● Recognize the difference between intrinsic arrhythmia and device-related rhythm behavior.
● Apply a basic rhythm interpretation sequence using rate, regularity, P waves, QRS width, and symptoms.
● Avoid common beginner errors during ECG rhythm interpretation.

Chapter Overview

Cardiac Arrhythmias

Cardiac arrhythmias refer to a group of conditions characterized by an irregular, too fast, or too slow heartbeat. These occur when the electrical impulses that coordinate heartbeats do not function properly, causing the heart to pump blood inefficiently.

 

 

 

1. Classification by Speed

  • Tachycardia: A resting heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute (bpm).
  • Bradycardia: A resting heart rate slower than 60 beats per minute.

The heart depends on a precise electrical system to maintain an effective pumping rhythm. Under normal conditions, electrical impulses begin in the sinoatrial (SA) node, travel through the atria, pause briefly in the atrioventricular (AV) node, and then spread rapidly through the ventricles.

When this electrical system becomes abnormal, the result is called an arrhythmia.

In simple terms:

Arrhythmia = Any abnormal heart rhythm, abnormal rate, irregular timing, or abnormal impulse conduction.

Arrhythmias can be:

●      Too slow (bradyarrhythmias)

●      Too fast (tachyarrhythmias)

●      Irregular

●      Intermittent

●      Life-threatening or benign

This chapter is highly relevant in cardiac rhythm management because pacemakers, ICDs, CRT systems, and monitoring technologies are all designed to detect or treat rhythm disorders.

 Arrhythmias can be:

● Too slow, known as bradyarrhythmias
● Too fast, known as tachyarrhythmias
● Irregular
● Intermittent
● Life-threatening or benign
● Symptomatic or asymptomatic
● Temporary or persistent
● Related to impulse formation or impulse conduction

This chapter is highly relevant in cardiac rhythm management because pacemakers, ICDs, CRT systems, and monitoring technologies are all designed to detect or treat rhythm disorders.

For pacemaker learners, bradyarrhythmias are especially important because pacemakers are commonly used to support slow or unreliable intrinsic heart rhythms.

Why Arrhythmias Matter

Abnormal rhythm may reduce cardiac output and cause symptoms such as:

●      Palpitations

●      Dizziness

●      Fatigue

●      Chest discomfort

●      Syncope

●      Shortness of breath

●      Sudden cardiac arrest (certain rhythms)

Some arrhythmias are discovered incidentally, while others require urgent treatment.

Main Categories of Cardiac Arrhythmias

1. Bradyarrhythmias

Slow heart rhythms (heart rate less than 60 bpm) due to:

●      Sinus node dysfunction

●      AV block

●      Escape rhythm failure

2. Tachyarrhythmias

Fast heart rhythms (heart rate more than 100 bpm)  such as:

●      Sinus tachycardia

●      SVT

●      Atrial flutter

●      Atrial fibrillation with RVR

●      Ventricular tachycardia
